newsitem.title: DUBAI: Nurses on trial in Saudi to sue U.S. lawyers.
newsitem.headline: Nurses on trial in Saudi to sue U.S. lawyers.

text.p: Two British nurses on trial for murder of an Australian colleague in Saudi Arabia have said they intended to bring suit against the U.S. law firm representing the family of the victim.

"Once this case has been concluded in Saudi Arabia, and our innocence established, we intend to bring suit against the American law firm of the Gilford family, Jones Day, for damages in the amount of $200 million," a statement signed by Lucille Mclauchlan and Deborah Parry said.

The statement, faxed to an international news agency in Dubai on Monday by defence lawyers, said the intended suit against would be brought for the U.S. firm's "ill-motivated and evil scheme to make our ordeal far worse than it would otherwise had been".

Parry, 38, and Mclauchlan, 31, are charged with murdering their 55-year-old colleague Yvonne Gilford in December at a medical complex in Dharan in the eastern province of Saudi Arabia. The women say they were forced to make confessions to the crime which they later withdrew. Both say they are innocent.
"It is shocking for these American lawyers to have turned their backs on Islamic traditions and to have deliberately ignored the court's direction for reconciliation," the statement said.

"The American lawyers have attempted to try us in the foreign and domestic media in complete disregard of the actual progress of the careful examination of any evidence by the duly authorised Public Prosecutor in Saudi Arabia," it added.
Defence lawyers said on Saturday they had submitted a legal paper to authorities outlining flaws in the case in order to have it dismissed.

The move came less than two weeks after the Islamic sharia court in the eastern Saudi city of Khobar adjourned for unspecified period for deliberation. At the last session on July 7, the family of the murdered nurse had insisted on the death sentence if the accused were found guilty.
The court had ruled earlier that Gilford's brother Frank had the right to demand execution if her alleged killers were found guilty as charged.

Islamic sharia law enforced in the kingdom gives the victim's heirs the right to decide for or against capital punishment if the court finds the accused guilty and says the death penalty is justified.
